properties.name: Read against the methods of proof: most fit an Inference's rule as built; discharged assumptions (contradiction, induction's step) and closed chains do not; evidence must never read as proof
properties.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_proof (section "Methods of proof"), read 2026-10-14 at Anthony's request
properties.statement:
Anthony asked how the article's types of proof come into play. Each was read against req:a-design-states-how-premises-support-a-conclusion-and-reflow2-checks-it-follows (C, being built) and this requirement (B).

FIT AN INFERENCE AS C BUILDS IT: rule `all` plus a rule_name.
- direct proof: a chain of inferences;
- induction: base case and inductive step give "for all n";
- contraposition: "not q implies not p" gives "p implies q";
- construction: a constructed example and its property give existence;
- exhaustion and case analysis. The premise "these cases are all the cases" must be a premise of its own. It is the one most often left out.
- the article's "combinatorial proof" is double counting: two counts of one set give an equality. It is NOT Hughes's combinatorial proofs from the earlier pasted text, so one term would carry two meanings.
- probabilistic method: a probability lemma gives existence with certainty;
- nonconstructive proof: usually a case split resting on the excluded middle. Recording that law as a premise shows which results depend on it.
The TWO-COLUMN PROOF (statement | reason) is exactly an Inference: the conclusion, and its rule or warrant.

NEED MORE THAN C:
1. DISCHARGED ASSUMPTIONS. Proof by contradiction assumes "√2 is rational", derives a contradiction, and concludes the opposite. Induction's step assumes P(k) to show P(k+1). Any "assume ... then" proof works the same way. The assumption is FALSE, or only local, and the final conclusion does NOT rest on it. C's rule, which needs premises that HOLD, would read such a proof as broken. B needs hypothetical sub-derivations: a premise role meaning "assumed for this sub-proof, discharged by this inference".
2. CLOSED CHAIN INFERENCE ("the following are equivalent": A ⇒ B ⇒ C ⇒ A) is a VALID cycle. It is not circular reasoning, because each implication is proven on its own and none of A, B, C is claimed true. Model the implications as statements of their own, so the support graph stays acyclic. C's cycle check must say this when it fires, not merely refuse.
3. EVIDENCE IS NOT PROOF. Statistical, heuristic and experimental mathematics, and flo2-calc evaluating cases, support a claim and never prove it. The ONE exception is exhaustion over a FINITE domain. "n² + n + 41 is prime for 0 ≤ n ≤ 39", checked in all 40 cases, IS proven by exhaustion. The same 40 cases are only evidence for "every n", which n = 40 refutes. B must keep deductive support apart from evidential support.

CONFIRMATION (B's "who confirmed"):
- a COMPUTER-ASSISTED proof (the four colour theorem's 1,936 cases, a proof assistant) is a step confirmed by a program. It fits a Verification implemented by that program, registered as an Artifact. reflow2's checksum drift then makes the confirmation STALE when the program changes, which is reproducibility for free.
- a VISUAL proof is a picture as warrant, confirmed by a person.
- an ELEMENTARY proof is a property of a proof, not a structure.

THE FAR END: an UNDECIDABLE statement is neither provable nor refutable from its axioms. That is a status distinct from "unknown" and "not yet proven". It is not needed before Navier–Stokes, if then.
